title: Limit of Detection (LOD) vs. Limit of Quantification (LOQ)

references.label: General microbiology/quantitative methods references (ASM, FDA BAM, CLSI)

summary: Two related but distinct analytical performance characteristics: the lowest amount of analyte that can be reliably distinguished from background (LOD), and the lowest amount that can be reliably and precisely measured, not merely detected (LOQ).
explanation: LOD answers 'is the analyte present at all, above background noise?' — it is a detection threshold, not a measurement threshold. LOQ answers a stricter question: 'at what level can I trust the actual numeric value the assay reports, with acceptable precision and accuracy?' LOQ is always at or above LOD, because reliably quantifying a signal requires a stronger signal-to-noise ratio than merely detecting that something is present. Reporting a result below LOQ but above LOD as a specific number (rather than as 'detected, below quantifiable range') overstates the confidence that specific number deserves.

comparison.example: Commonly estimated as blank mean + 3×SD of the blank
Commonly estimated as blank mean + 10×SD of the blank (a larger multiplier, reflecting the stricter precision requirement)

commonMisconceptions: Treating LOD and LOQ as interchangeable — a result can be reliably detected without being reliably quantifiable.
Reporting a precise numeric value for a signal that falls between LOD and LOQ, implying more quantitative confidence than that range actually supports.
